lesson.title: The Map of States: Reading a Phase Diagram
lesson.summary: A phase diagram plots pressure against temperature and shows exactly which phase, or combination of coexisting phases, is stable at any given condition, anchored by the triple point and the critical point.
lesson.body:
A phase diagram is a two dimensional map, temperature on one axis and pressure on the other, that shows which phase, solid, liquid, or gas, is stable at every possible combination of temperature and pressure for a given substance. The map is divided into three regions by three curves: a solid liquid boundary, the melting and freezing curve, a liquid gas boundary, the boiling and condensation curve, also called the vapor pressure curve, and a solid gas boundary, the sublimation and deposition curve. Crossing any of these curves, by changing temperature or pressure, corresponds exactly to one of the phase changes discussed throughout this unit.

The three curves all meet at one special point, the triple point, the unique combination of temperature and pressure at which solid, liquid, and gas all coexist simultaneously in equilibrium. For water, the triple point sits at 0.01 C and a pressure of about 4.58 mmHg. The liquid gas boundary does not extend forever, either: it terminates at the critical point, above which the distinction between liquid and gas disappears entirely into a single supercritical fluid phase. For water, the critical point is at about 374 C and 218 atm.

One especially useful feature of a phase diagram is that it directly explains why some substances sublime under normal conditions while others melt first. Draw a horizontal line across the diagram at 1 atm, ordinary atmospheric pressure, and trace it from low temperature to high temperature. Whether that line passes through the liquid region at all, or skips straight from solid to gas, depends entirely on whether the triple point pressure is above or below 1 atm.

Water's triple point pressure, 4.58 mmHg, converts to atm by dividing by 760 mmHg per atm: 4.58 divided by 760 equals about 0.00603 atm. Comparing that to standard atmospheric pressure: 1.00 atm divided by 0.00603 atm is about 166, meaning atmospheric pressure is roughly 166 times higher than water's triple point pressure. Since the horizontal line at 1 atm sits far above the triple point, it necessarily crosses the solid liquid melting curve before it could ever reach a low enough pressure to cross the sublimation curve instead, which is exactly why ice melts into liquid water on the way to becoming steam at ordinary atmospheric pressure, rather than subliming directly. Carbon dioxide tells the opposite story: its triple point pressure is about 5.11 atm, above atmospheric pressure, so the 1 atm horizontal line sits below the triple point entirely and never enters the liquid region at all; it only crosses the sublimation curve, which is exactly why dry ice sublimes instead of melting under normal conditions, consistent with what was described in the sublimation and deposition chapter. To get liquid CO2 at all, you would need to raise the pressure to at least 5.11 atm, more than five times atmospheric pressure, before a liquid region even becomes accessible on the map.
